q: Gini vs entropy: which and why?
a: Both measure impurity and usually choose very similar splits. Gini (default in sklearn) is slightly faster because there's no logarithm. Entropy is a bit more sensitive to changes in class probabilities and tends to produce slightly more balanced trees. In practice, tune depth and leaf size; the criterion rarely matters.

q: How does a tree split a continuous feature?
a: Sort the unique values, try a threshold at each midpoint between consecutive values, compute the impurity gain for each, keep the best. Libraries like XGBoost and LightGBM use histogram bins instead to save time.

No. Each leaf predicts the mean of its training targets, so predictions are bounded by the training range. If house prices in training go up to ₹2 Cr, a ₹5 Cr house is still predicted at about ₹2 Cr. Same for Random Forest and boosting. Use linear models or add trend features for extrapolation.

q: How do you prevent a decision tree from overfitting?
a: Pre-pruning: max_depth, min_samples_leaf, min_samples_split, max_leaf_nodes, min_impurity_decrease. Post-pruning: grow fully then prune with cost-complexity pruning (ccp_alpha), chosen by cross-validation. Or use an ensemble.

q: Why do decision trees have high variance?
a: Splits are greedy and hierarchical. A small change in the data can change the root split, and every split below it changes too, giving a completely different tree. That's why averaging many trees (bagging, Random Forest) works so well.

q: Do trees need feature scaling or one-hot encoding?
a: No scaling: splits depend only on the order of values. One-hot is optional and often worse for high-cardinality features (many sparse weak splits). Ordinal, frequency or target encoding, or native categorical support, usually works better.

q: Information gain is biased toward which features? How is that fixed?
a: Features with many distinct values (like an ID column) can split data into tiny pure groups and get very high information gain while being useless. C4.5 uses gain ratio (gain divided by split information) to correct this.

ID3: categorical features, entropy/information gain, multi-way splits. C4.5: adds continuous features, gain ratio, missing values, pruning. CART (used by sklearn): binary splits only, Gini for classification and MSE for regression, cost-complexity pruning.

q: What's the time complexity of training a tree?
a: Roughly \(O(p \cdot n \log n)\) per level (sorting each feature), about \(O(p\, n \log^2 n)\) for a balanced tree overall. Prediction is \(O(\text{depth})\).

q: Your data has a diagonal boundary (y > x). Why does a tree struggle?
a: Splits are axis-aligned, so the tree approximates a diagonal with a staircase of many splits. Fix with a feature like x − y, a rotation (PCA), or a model that learns oblique boundaries (logistic regression, SVM).

q: How does a decision tree handle missing values?
a: Depends on the implementation. CART can use surrogate splits (a backup feature that mimics the primary split). sklearn (≥ 1.3) learns which side to send missing values. XGBoost/LightGBM learn a default direction. Otherwise impute and add a missing flag.
